title: Tennessee’s Koby Bujak-Upton Drops Three Lifetime Bests Ahead of High-Stakes Australian Trials
summary: Timing is everything in swimming, and Koby Bujak-Upton’s timing couldn’t be better. The Tennessee sophomore — who made history last season as the first freshman to break 1:30 in the 200-yard freestyle — just delivered a statement performance at the MAC Charlotte Open, clocking lifetime bests in all three sprint freestyle distances. With the Australian Trials looming next week in Sydney, Bujak-Upton is riding a wave of momentum. In Charlotte, he sliced three-tenths off his 50 free, touching in 22.90 — a significant drop from his previous best of 23.20 set in April 2024. He also lowered his 100 free to 48.96 (down from 49.66) and his 200 free to 1:48.44 (previously 1:48.74). Those improvements may seem marginal, but at the elite level, they’re the difference between a podium finish and watching from the stands. Bujak-Upton’s freshman campaign was already the stuff of legend. At the NCAA Championships, he placed second in the 200 free with a 1:30.11, cementing his status as one of just nine college swimmers ever to go sub-1:30 in the event. Now, he’ll test his long-course speed against Australia’s best, entered in all three sprint freestyle events at Trials. But the Charlotte meet wasn’t a one-man show. Sixteen-year-old David Sammons erupted with a slew of personal bests, including a 200 IM (2:03.70), 400 IM (4:20.65), and a 200 fly (1:57.98) that ranks him ninth all-time in the U.S. 15-16 age group. His 400 IM tied for 12th in the same age group’s national rankings. Sammons also notched bests in the 50 fly and 200 back, proving he’s a name to watch. Tennessee’s Lexi Stephens added to the haul with backstroke wins (1:01.40 in the 100, 2:13.60 in the 200), just off her lifetime bests. As the swimming world turns its eyes to Sydney, one question lingers: can Bujak-Upton translate his short-course brilliance to the long-course pool and punch his ticket to the biggest stage?
why_it_matters: For middle-schoolers, Bujak-Upton’s story shows that tiny, almost invisible improvements — just three-tenths of a second — can be the difference between making a national team and staying home, and that consistent hard work creates opportunities when the biggest moments arrive.

background_read: NCAA swimming in the United States uses 25-yard 'short-course' pools, while the Australian Trials and the Olympics use 50-meter 'long-course' pools; swimmers must adjust their turns, pacing, and race strategy when switching between the two.

Australia has a deep swimming tradition, having produced legends like Ian Thorpe and Emma McKeon; making the national team at Trials is fiercely competitive because only the top finishers earn spots at the World Championships or Olympics.

Koby Bujak-Upton, who holds dual citizenship with Australia and the United States, could be aiming to represent Australia at the Paris 2024 Olympics or future World Aquatics Championships, making these Trials a crucial career stepping stone.
At the NCAA Championships, he finished second in the 200-yard free and became only the ninth swimmer in college history to dip under 1:30 — a barrier-breaking moment for a freshman.

perspectives.description: Dropping time across all three sprint events signals that he is peaking at exactly the right moment, giving him a strong chance to qualify for Australia’s senior national team and gain international experience.

High-stakes meets like Trials bring enormous psychological pressure, and the shift from short-course yards to long-course meters is not guaranteed; even tiny mistakes in turns or pacing could cost him a spot.

Swimming success depends on periodization — training cycles designed to peak at a specific meet. The NCAA season operates in yards, while international swimming uses meters, so athletes who excel in both systems must carefully manage their training and race plans.
If Bujak-Upton makes the Australian team, he could join a new generation of sprint talent and eventually target Olympic medals, helping to reshape the future of Australian men's freestyle swimming.
